question.text: How far ahead should you read the road, and why?

answer.text: Keep your eyes moving and read the road about one city block ahead, so you are not forced into last-minute decisions.

teaching.text: Keep your eyes moving and look about a city block down the road, so you are never stuck making last-second choices. Remember: one city block ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep your eyes moving and read the road about one city block ahead, so you are not forced into last-minute decisions.

question.text: How does the block-ahead rule differ from the following-distance count?

answer.text: Looking about one city block ahead is the scanning rule, and it is separate from the seconds-based count used for following distance.

teaching.text: Looking a city block ahead is about scanning, and it is a different rule from the seconds count for following distance. Remember: look far, count gap.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Looking about one city block ahead is the scanning rule, and it is separate from the seconds-based count used for following distance.

question.text: What should you do as you approach an intersection?

answer.text: As you approach an intersection, look both left and right before you continue.

teaching.text: As you near an intersection, look to the left and to the right before you go on. Remember: look left, look right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: As you approach an intersection, look both left and right before you continue.

question.text: What does checking your rearview mirror often tell you?

answer.text: Checking the rearview mirror often shows you where traffic behind you is and warns you when someone is tailgating or closing in too fast.

teaching.text: Frequent glances in the rearview mirror show where traffic behind you is and warn you of tailgaters or fast-closing vehicles. Remember: watch who follows.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Checking the rearview mirror often shows you where traffic behind you is and warns you when someone is tailgating or closing in too fast.

question.text: What two checks come before a lane change?

answer.text: Before a lane change, check the side mirrors and also turn your head to look over your shoulder.

teaching.text: Before moving to another lane, check the side mirrors and also turn your head for a look over your shoulder. Remember: mirrors plus shoulder.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before a lane change, check the side mirrors and also turn your head to look over your shoulder.

question.text: What lets you make decisions quickly and safely in traffic?

answer.text: When you keep track of how fast and where the traffic is in front, behind and on both sides, you can make decisions quickly and safely.

teaching.text: Knowing the speed and position of traffic ahead, behind and on each side lets you make quick, safe decisions. Remember: track traffic all around.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When you keep track of how fast and where the traffic is in front, behind and on both sides, you can make decisions quickly and safely.

question.text: How do you test whether you are following too closely?

answer.text: The manual's three-six second rule tests your gap: when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point such as a sign or overpass, start counting, and if you reach that point before you finish, you are following too closely.

teaching.text: When the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point like a sign, start counting; if you reach that point before the count ends, you are too close. Remember: pick a point, count.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The manual's three-six second rule tests your gap: when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point such as a sign or overpass, start counting, and if you reach that point before you finish, you are following too closely.

question.text: About how long does it take to count from one-thousand-one to one-thousand-four?

answer.text: Counting from one-thousand-one to one-thousand-four takes about four seconds.

teaching.text: Counting from one-thousand-one through one-thousand-four takes roughly four seconds. Remember: four counts, four seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Counting from one-thousand-one to one-thousand-four takes about four seconds.

question.text: How does the four-second example count differ from the poor-conditions cushion?

answer.text: The count in the example runs to four and takes about four seconds, while the cushion the manual recommends in poor conditions spans three to six seconds.

teaching.text: The example count to four lasts about four seconds, while the poor-conditions cushion is a range of three to six seconds. Remember: example four, cushion three to six.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The count in the example runs to four and takes about four seconds, while the cushion the manual recommends in poor conditions spans three to six seconds.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: example four, cushion three to six

question.text: How should your following distance change as your speed rises?

answer.text: The faster you go, the greater your following distance should be.

teaching.text: Leave more following distance the faster you are going. Remember: faster means farther back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The faster you go, the greater your following distance should be.

question.text: How much cushion should you leave in poor road conditions?

answer.text: Poor road conditions call for more than a three-second cushion, so give yourself three to six seconds.

teaching.text: On poor roads a three-second gap is not enough, so leave three to six seconds. Remember: three to six seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Poor road conditions call for more than a three-second cushion, so give yourself three to six seconds.

question.text: Why does high speed shrink your margin for error?

answer.text: At high speed you travel farther while reacting to a problem, so your margin for error shrinks.

teaching.text: At high speed you cover more ground while reacting, so there is less room for error. Remember: speed eats reaction room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At high speed you travel farther while reacting to a problem, so your margin for error shrinks.

question.text: What causes most rear-end crashes?

answer.text: Following too closely causes most rear-end crashes.

teaching.text: Most rear-end crashes come from following too closely. Remember: tailgating causes rear-enders.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Following too closely causes most rear-end crashes.

question.text: Why does space around your vehicle matter, and where in the lane should you stay?

answer.text: Space around your vehicle gives you and other drivers time to react to emergencies, and staying in the middle of your lane helps create that cushion.

teaching.text: Space around your car gives everyone time to react to an emergency, and keeping to the middle of your lane builds that cushion. Remember: middle of the lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Space around your vehicle gives you and other drivers time to react to emergencies, and staying in the middle of your lane helps create that cushion.

question.text: How much room should you keep ahead of and behind your vehicle?

answer.text: Keep enough room ahead of you to stop suddenly, and enough room ahead and behind to pass or stop safely.

teaching.text: Leave enough room ahead to stop suddenly, and enough ahead and behind to pass or stop safely. Remember: room to stop or pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep enough room ahead of you to stop suddenly, and enough room ahead and behind to pass or stop safely.

question.text: How much room must you give a bicycle when you share a lane?

answer.text: When you share a lane with a bicycle, keep at least three feet between your vehicle and the rider and moderate your speed.

teaching.text: When a bicycle shares your lane, keep at least three feet from the rider and ease your speed. Remember: three feet and slower.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When you share a lane with a bicycle, keep at least three feet between your vehicle and the rider and moderate your speed.

question.text: How is following distance measured compared with bicycle clearance?

answer.text: Following distance is counted in seconds behind the vehicle ahead, while bicycle clearance in a shared lane is a fixed three feet to the side.

teaching.text: Following distance is timed in seconds behind you, while bicycle room is a fixed three feet beside you. Remember: seconds behind, feet beside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Following distance is counted in seconds behind the vehicle ahead, while bicycle clearance in a shared lane is a fixed three feet to the side.

question.text: How can you help the driver behind you keep a safe gap?

answer.text: You help the driver behind you keep a safe gap by holding a steady speed and signaling early before you slow down or stop.

teaching.text: Hold a steady speed and signal early before slowing or stopping, so the driver behind you can keep a safe gap. Remember: steady speed, early signal.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You help the driver behind you keep a safe gap by holding a steady speed and signaling early before you slow down or stop.

question.text: What should you do if someone is tailgating you?

answer.text: If someone is tailgating you, slow down gradually and open more space ahead, so you can brake more gently and give the tailgater time to react.

teaching.text: With a tailgater behind you, slow gradually and leave extra space ahead, so you can brake gently and the tailgater has time to react. Remember: ease off, add space.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If someone is tailgating you, slow down gradually and open more space ahead, so you can brake more gently and give the tailgater time to react.

question.text: What is the right response to a tailgater?

answer.text: A tailgater is handled by slowing gradually and adding space ahead of you, which lets you brake more gently when you must stop.

teaching.text: The answer to a tailgater is to slow gradually and add space ahead, so you can brake gently if you must stop. Remember: slow gently, add space.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A tailgater is handled by slowing gradually and adding space ahead of you, which lets you brake more gently when you must stop.

question.text: What else can encourage a tailgater to go around you?

answer.text: When it is safe, changing to another lane encourages a tailgater to go around you.

teaching.text: When it is safe, moving to another lane encourages a tailgater to pass you. Remember: move over if safe.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When it is safe, changing to another lane encourages a tailgater to go around you.

question.text: Whose safety do your actions affect when you stop suddenly?

answer.text: What you do affects the driver behind you, especially when you have to stop suddenly.

teaching.text: Your actions affect the driver behind you, most of all when you must stop suddenly. Remember: think of who follows.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: What you do affects the driver behind you, especially when you have to stop suddenly.

question.text: What are blind spots?

answer.text: Blind spots are the areas at the left and right sides of your vehicle that your mirrors do not show.

teaching.text: Blind spots are the areas on the left and right sides of your car that your mirrors do not show. Remember: where mirrors miss.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Blind spots are the areas at the left and right sides of your vehicle that your mirrors do not show.

question.text: What should you do when parked cars or bushes block your view at an intersection?

answer.text: When cars parked near an intersection or bushes, trees or buildings block your view, creep forward slowly until you can see clearly, then go when the way is clear.

teaching.text: If parked cars, bushes, trees or buildings block your view, ease forward slowly until you can see, then go when it is clear. Remember: creep, see, then go.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When cars parked near an intersection or bushes, trees or buildings block your view, creep forward slowly until you can see clearly, then go when the way is clear.

question.text: How do you stay out of other drivers' blind spots?

answer.text: Stay out of other drivers' blind spots, watching for motorcycles too, by speeding up or dropping back rather than lingering beside them.

teaching.text: Do not ride in another driver's blind spot; speed up or drop back, and watch for motorcycles too. Remember: do not linger beside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stay out of other drivers' blind spots, watching for motorcycles too, by speeding up or dropping back rather than lingering beside them.

question.text: Why should you not rely on your mirrors alone?

answer.text: Make sure other drivers can see your vehicle, and do not trust your mirrors alone to show vehicles or motorcycles beside you.

teaching.text: Make sure other drivers can see you, and never rely on mirrors alone to show vehicles or motorcycles beside you. Remember: be seen, look yourself.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Make sure other drivers can see your vehicle, and do not trust your mirrors alone to show vehicles or motorcycles beside you.

question.text: What should you do to confirm the way is clear before changing lanes?

answer.text: Look over your shoulder to confirm the way is clear before changing lanes.

teaching.text: Before changing lanes, look over your shoulder to make sure the way is clear. Remember: look over your shoulder.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Look over your shoulder to confirm the way is clear before changing lanes.

question.text: How do you deal with your blind spots compared with other drivers' blind spots?

answer.text: Your own blind spots are cleared with a shoulder check, while other drivers' blind spots are avoided by speeding up or dropping back.

teaching.text: Clear your own blind spots with a shoulder check, and stay out of other drivers' by speeding up or dropping back. Remember: check yours, avoid theirs.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your own blind spots are cleared with a shoulder check, while other drivers' blind spots are avoided by speeding up or dropping back.

question.text: What should you do when entering a road from a private drive?

answer.text: When entering the road from a side road or a private drive, stop and wait until traffic clears.

teaching.text: When pulling onto a road from a side road or private drive, stop and wait for traffic to clear. Remember: stop, wait, then enter.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When entering the road from a side road or a private drive, stop and wait until traffic clears.

question.text: Should you pull out because an oncoming vehicle has its turn signal on?

answer.text: Do not assume a vehicle or motorcycle with its turn signal on will really turn; wait until you see the driver commit to the turn before you pull out.

teaching.text: A blinking turn signal is not proof; wait until you see the other driver actually commit to the turn before you pull out. Remember: wait for the turn.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not assume a vehicle or motorcycle with its turn signal on will really turn; wait until you see the driver commit to the turn before you pull out.

question.text: Does another driver's blinking signal give you a gap to enter?

answer.text: Entering from a private drive means stopping and waiting for a clear gap, and another driver's blinking signal does not create that gap.

teaching.text: Leaving a private drive means waiting for a real gap; another driver's blinking signal does not make one. Remember: signals are not gaps.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Entering from a private drive means stopping and waiting for a clear gap, and another driver's blinking signal does not create that gap.

question.text: When should you use your turn signals?

answer.text: Use your turn signals whenever you change direction, such as moving to another lane, turning at an intersection, merging onto a freeway, leaving a curb or pulling off the road.

teaching.text: Signal every change of direction, including lane changes, turns, merging onto a freeway, leaving a curb and pulling off the road. Remember: every change of direction.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use your turn signals whenever you change direction, such as moving to another lane, turning at an intersection, merging onto a freeway, leaving a curb or pulling off the road.

question.text: Why signal even when no one seems to be around?

answer.text: Signal out of habit even when no one else seems to be around, because the vehicle or motorcycle you have not noticed poses the greatest danger.

teaching.text: Signal by habit even on an empty road, because the vehicle you did not notice is the biggest danger. Remember: the unseen car matters.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signal out of habit even when no one else seems to be around, because the vehicle or motorcycle you have not noticed poses the greatest danger.

question.text: What does communicating mean for a driver?

answer.text: Communicating means showing other drivers and pedestrians what you intend to do early enough to prevent a collision.

teaching.text: Communicating means letting drivers and pedestrians know what you will do early enough to prevent a crash. Remember: show intentions early.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Communicating means showing other drivers and pedestrians what you intend to do early enough to prevent a collision.

question.text: How far before a turn should you signal?

answer.text: Signal at least one hundred feet, roughly four seconds, before you turn so others have time to react.

teaching.text: Turn on your signal at least one hundred feet, about four seconds, before the turn so others can react. Remember: one hundred feet ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signal at least one hundred feet, roughly four seconds, before you turn so others have time to react.

question.text: About how many seconds of driving is the signaling distance?

answer.text: The turn-signal distance is one hundred feet, which the manual puts at about four seconds of driving.

teaching.text: The signaling distance of one hundred feet works out to about four seconds of driving. Remember: about four seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The turn-signal distance is one hundred feet, which the manual puts at about four seconds of driving.

question.text: What does the law set for turns and signaling?

answer.text: The law sets the lanes and positions you must use for turns and requires a signal at least one hundred feet before you turn.

teaching.text: The law decides which lanes and positions you use for turns and requires signaling at least one hundred feet before turning. Remember: lanes, positions, one hundred feet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The law sets the lanes and positions you must use for turns and requires a signal at least one hundred feet before you turn.

question.text: When should you signal for a turn that comes just past an intersection?

answer.text: If your turn comes just past an intersection, wait until you are inside the intersection to signal, because drivers there could pull into your path.

teaching.text: If your turn is just beyond an intersection, wait until you are inside the intersection to signal, so drivers there do not pull out in front of you. Remember: signal inside the intersection.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If your turn comes just past an intersection, wait until you are inside the intersection to signal, because drivers there could pull into your path.

question.text: How does signaling for a turn just past an intersection break the usual rule?

answer.text: For a turn just past an intersection you hold the signal until you are inside the intersection, the opposite of the usual rule to signal well ahead.

teaching.text: A turn just past an intersection is the exception: hold the signal until you are inside the intersection. Remember: wait until inside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a turn just past an intersection you hold the signal until you are inside the intersection, the opposite of the usual rule to signal well ahead.

question.text: What should you check after finishing a turn or lane change?

answer.text: After you finish your move, make sure the turn signal has gone off.

teaching.text: Once the move is finished, check that your turn signal has shut off. Remember: signal off after.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After you finish your move, make sure the turn signal has gone off.

question.text: Does signaling give you the right-of-way?

answer.text: A signal warns others of your move and gives them time to react, but it does not give you the right-of-way.

teaching.text: A signal warns others and buys them time, but it never gives you the right-of-way. Remember: signals warn, not win.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A signal warns others of your move and gives them time to react, but it does not give you the right-of-way.

question.text: What ways may you use to show a turn?

answer.text: You may show a turn with your turn signals, with hand signals, or with both.

teaching.text: You can show a turn with your turn signals, with hand signals, or with both. Remember: lights, hands, or both.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You may show a turn with your turn signals, with hand signals, or with both.

question.text: Which moves always call for a signal?

answer.text: Always signal before changing lanes, turning at an intersection or into a driveway or alley, entering or leaving a freeway, pulling away from the curb, or pulling over to the side of the road.

teaching.text: Always signal before changing lanes, turning at an intersection or into a driveway or alley, using a freeway ramp, leaving the curb or pulling over. Remember: signal every move.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always signal before changing lanes, turning at an intersection or into a driveway or alley, entering or leaving a freeway, pulling away from the curb, or pulling over to the side of the road.

question.text: When using hand signals, what else must you signal?

answer.text: When you are using hand signals, also signal before you slow down or stop suddenly.

teaching.text: If you are using hand signals, also signal before you slow down or stop suddenly. Remember: hand signal before stopping.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When you are using hand signals, also signal before you slow down or stop suddenly.

question.text: What extra case do hand signals cover?

answer.text: Hand signals add one case the turn-signal list does not: signaling before you slow down or stop suddenly.

teaching.text: Hand signals add one case the turn-signal list does not cover: signaling before you slow down or stop suddenly. Remember: hand signal for slowing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hand signals add one case the turn-signal list does not: signaling before you slow down or stop suddenly.

question.text: How do you pass a vehicle going your way?

answer.text: To pass a vehicle or motorcycle going your way, signal the lane change and pass on the left.

teaching.text: To get around a vehicle going your way, signal the lane change and pass on the left. Remember: signal, pass on the left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To pass a vehicle or motorcycle going your way, signal the lane change and pass on the left.

question.text: What must you be sure of before passing?

answer.text: Before passing, be sure you have the time and room to get completely ahead of the other vehicle without endangering oncoming traffic.

teaching.text: Only pass when you have enough time and room to get fully ahead without putting oncoming traffic at risk. Remember: time and room first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before passing, be sure you have the time and room to get completely ahead of the other vehicle without endangering oncoming traffic.

question.text: When may you return to the right lane after passing?

answer.text: Return to the right lane once you can see the whole front, or both headlights, of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror, after a shoulder check and a signal.

teaching.text: Move back into the right lane when the whole front, or both headlights, of the passed vehicle shows in your rearview mirror, after a shoulder check and a signal. Remember: both headlights in mirror.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Return to the right lane once you can see the whole front, or both headlights, of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror, after a shoulder check and a signal.

question.text: What cue tells you it is safe to return after passing?

answer.text: The cue for returning to the right lane is seeing the whole front or both headlights of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.

teaching.text: The signal to move back after passing is seeing the passed vehicle's whole front or both headlights in your rearview mirror. Remember: whole front in mirror.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The cue for returning to the right lane is seeing the whole front or both headlights of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.

question.text: Do the passing steps change for slow motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds?

answer.text: The same passing steps apply when you pass slow-moving motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds.

teaching.text: Use the same passing steps for slow motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds. Remember: same steps for all.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The same passing steps apply when you pass slow-moving motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds.

question.text: What should you do when a vehicle behind you wants to pass?

answer.text: If a vehicle behind you honks or flashes its lights to pass, move right when it is safe and let it by, and never speed up while you are being passed.

teaching.text: If a driver behind you honks or flashes to pass, move right when safe, let them by, and never speed up. Remember: move right, let it by.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If a vehicle behind you honks or flashes its lights to pass, move right when it is safe and let it by, and never speed up while you are being passed.

question.text: What must you never do while being passed?

answer.text: Being passed calls for moving right when it is safe and letting the other vehicle by; speeding up while being passed is never allowed.

teaching.text: When someone passes you, move right if safe and let them go by; speeding up is never allowed. Remember: never speed up.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Being passed calls for moving right when it is safe and letting the other vehicle by; speeding up while being passed is never allowed.

question.text: When may you pass on the right?

answer.text: Passing on the right is allowed only when it is safe and the other driver is turning left, and you must never pass on the left of a driver who has signaled a left turn.

teaching.text: You may pass on the right only when it is safe and the driver ahead is turning left, and never pass on the left of a signaled left turner. Remember: right only around left-turners.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing on the right is allowed only when it is safe and the other driver is turning left, and you must never pass on the left of a driver who has signaled a left turn.

question.text: Where else may you pass on the right?

answer.text: Passing on the right is also allowed on an open highway clearly marked for two or more lanes moving in your direction.

teaching.text: Passing on the right is also allowed on an open highway marked for two or more lanes going your way. Remember: multi-lane highways too.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing on the right is also allowed on an open highway clearly marked for two or more lanes moving in your direction.

question.text: When is passing on the right allowed instead of the left?

answer.text: Normal passing is on the left; passing on the right needs both safety and a listed condition such as a driver ahead who is turning left.

teaching.text: Passing is normally on the left, and passing on the right needs safety plus a listed condition such as a left-turning driver ahead. Remember: left normal, right conditional.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Normal passing is on the left; passing on the right needs both safety and a listed condition such as a driver ahead who is turning left.

hooks_spoken: Look a block ahead, check left and right at intersections, and use mirrors and a shoulder check before changing lanes.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of scanning the road. Look a block ahead, check left and right at intersections, and use mirrors and a shoulder check before changing lanes. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Count from a fixed point to test your gap, and add more distance at higher speed and in poor conditions.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of following distance. Count from a fixed point to test your gap, and add more distance at higher speed and in poor conditions. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Keep space all around, give a bicycle three feet, and slow gradually for a tailgater.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of space cushion and tailgaters. Keep space all around, give a bicycle three feet, and slow gradually for a tailgater. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Shoulder-check your own blind spots, stay out of others', and never pull out on a turn signal alone.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of blind spots and entering traffic. Shoulder-check your own blind spots, stay out of others', and never pull out on a turn signal alone. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Signal every move about one hundred feet ahead, but remember that a signal never gives you the right-of-way.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of signaling your moves. Signal every move about one hundred feet ahead, but remember that a signal never gives you the right-of-way. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Pass on the left with time and room, return when both headlights show in your mirror, and never speed up while being passed.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of passing safely. Pass on the left with time and room, return when both headlights show in your mirror, and never speed up while being passed. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.
